query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX alloys (with X = Al, Mn, or Si), the formation and persistence of a stable, coherent protective oxide above 900 °C is governed by the ability of the alloy to form a continuous, chemically compatible Cr‐Al rich sub-oxide layer. Alloys with sufficient Al content develop an adherent, slow-growing mixed chromium–alumina protective scale that minimizes thermal stresses and oxygen ingress, whereas those with higher Mn or Si contents form defective oxides prone to cracking and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy fabricated as a single or multiphase metallic solid-solution using techniques such as arc melting and homogenization annealing; the baseline is defined as an alloy with lower Al content (and relatively higher Mn or Si) known to form unstable oxide layers.
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of the X element – specifically increasing Al content relative to Mn or Si – to assess the effect on protective oxide formation.
generation.conditions: Exposure to temperatures above 900 °C (e.g., 950–1000 °C) for prolonged durations (100–200 hours) in an oxidative atmosphere (e.g., ambient air or controlled oxygen partial pressures) or in mildly corrosive environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A coherent Cr–Al oxide sublayer that forms at the metal/oxide interface, presenting low defect density and a thermal expansion match with the substrate.
generation.mechanism: The oxidation mechanism involves rapid reactive formation of Cr and Al oxides, where the presence of adequate Al facilitates the development of a slow-growing, adherent alumina-based layer that acts as a barrier to further oxygen ingress. The compatibility of this mixed oxide with the substrate minimizes thermal mismatch stresses, reducing cracking and spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with elevated Al content will show the formation of a thin, continuous, and adherent protective oxide layer at high temperature, leading to reduced oxide scale cracking and spallation compared with alloys richer in Mn or Si.
generation.baseline: CrFeCoNiX alloys with lower Al content (and higher Mn or Si) that are known to develop unstable, cracked, or spalled oxide layers when exposed to high temperatures in oxidative or corrosive environments.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under conditions of high-temperature exposure (above 900 °C) in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres and remains valid for alloys retaining a single or multiphase metallic solid-solution microstructure without significant segregation or secondary phase formation.
generation.uncertainty: The individual roles of Si and Mn in altering oxidation kinetics and thermal stress development remain uncertain, and their effects may interact with Al content in complex ways that require further quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of CrFeCoNiX alloys with systematically varied X content (e.g., Al-rich, Mn-rich, Si-rich) using consistent processing methods (arc melting, homogenization annealing). Expose these specimens to 950 °C in an oxidative atmosphere (ambient air or controlled oxygen level) for 150 hours followed by thermal cycling tests. Characterize the resulting oxide layers using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and X-ray diffraction (XRD), and measure adhesion strength and crack density.
measurements: Phase composition of the oxide (via XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if Al-rich compositions do not display significantly improved oxide scale coherence, reduced spallation, and lower cracking incidence compared to Mn- or Si-rich compositions under identical high-temperature and oxidative conditions.
